articleHeader.title: What is Python Programming Language?
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete beginner-friendly guide to Python — covering history, features, how Python works, CPython interpreter, OOP concepts, Hello World program, and why Python is the #1 language to learn in 2026.

blocks.text: Python is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted programming language known for its clean, readable syntax and beginner-friendly design. It was created by Guido van Rossum and officially released on February 20, 1991. The Python Software Foundation (PSF) currently maintains and oversees the language.

Python follows the philosophy of "There should be one — and preferably only one — obvious way to do it", as described in the famous Zen of Python. Python code is designed to be readable and expressive — a well-written Python program often reads almost like plain English. This makes it the most beginner-friendly language available today.

Python is both a programming language and an ecosystem. The language itself is simple and concise, but its true power comes from an enormous standard library and over 450,000 third-party packages on PyPI (Python Package Index). This dual nature is one of the key reasons Python dominates fields from web development to artificial intelligence.

According to the TIOBE Index 2026 and Stack Overflow Developer Survey, Python has been the #1 most popular programming language for several consecutive years. It is the language of choice for AI and machine learning, data science, web backend development, automation and scripting, and scientific computing.

The story of Python begins in the late 1980s at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands. Guido van Rossum started working on Python as a hobby project during Christmas 1989, aiming to create a successor to the ABC language that could handle exceptions and interface with the Amoeba operating system. The name "Python" was inspired by the British comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus — not the snake.

items.text: — Python 0.9.0 released. First public version included classes with inheritance, exception handling, functions, and the core built-in types.
— Python 1.0 released. Added functional programming tools like lambda, map, filter, and reduce.
— Python 2.0 released. Introduced list comprehensions, garbage collection, and Unicode support.
— Python 3.0 (Python 3000) released — a major backward-incompatible redesign that fixed fundamental flaws in Python 2. Print became a function, integers unified, strings became Unicode by default.
— Python 2 officially reached end-of-life (January 1, 2020). All developers migrated to Python 3.
— Python 3.10 released. Introduced structural pattern matching (match/case) — Python's most powerful new syntax in years.
— Python 3.12 released. Significant performance improvements (up to 25% faster), better error messages, and f-string enhancements.
— Python 3.13 and 3.14 released. Experimental free-threaded mode (no GIL), JIT compiler preview, and continued performance improvements. Python 3.13+ is the recommended version in 2026.

sections.title: Key Features of Python Programming Language

blocks.text: Python's dominance across so many fields is no accident. Its design philosophy prioritises developer experience and code readability above everything else. Here are the 13 core features that define Python:

items.title: Easy to Read & Write
items.text: Python's clean syntax uses indentation instead of braces. Code reads almost like plain English — making it the #1 choice for beginners and the fastest language for prototyping ideas.

items.title: Interpreted
items.text: Python code is executed line-by-line by the interpreter. No separate compilation step needed — write code and run it immediately, making debugging and experimentation effortless.

items.title: Cross-Platform
items.text: The same Python script runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS without modification. Install Python once, run your code anywhere — similar in spirit to Java's WORA principle.

items.title: Dynamically Typed
items.text: No need to declare variable types — Python infers them at runtime. x = 5 makes x an int automatically. This speeds up development but requires careful testing.

items.title: Multi-Paradigm
items.text: Python supports Object-Oriented, Functional, and Procedural programming styles. You can use classes and objects, or write simple scripts — Python never forces one approach.

items.title: Massive Ecosystem
items.text: PyPI hosts 450,000+ packages. NumPy, Pandas, TensorFlow, Django, Flask, FastAPI — whatever you need, there is a Python library for it. pip install and you're ready.

items.title: Automatic Memory Management
items.text: Python's garbage collector automatically manages memory using reference counting plus a cyclic GC. Developers never need to manually allocate or free memory.

items.title: Extensible & Embeddable
items.text: Python can call C/C++ libraries for performance-critical code. Conversely, Python can be embedded inside C/C++ applications as a scripting engine.

items.title: Supports Concurrency
items.text: Python supports threading, multiprocessing, and async/await (asyncio). Python 3.13+ offers an experimental free-threaded mode that removes the GIL for true multi-core parallelism.

items.title: Excellent for Prototyping
items.text: Python's concise syntax means you write 3-5x fewer lines than Java or C++ for the same functionality. Ideal for testing ideas, building MVPs, and rapid iteration.

items.title: AI/ML Powerhouse
items.text: Python is the universal language of artificial intelligence. TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn, Keras, and Hugging Face Transformers are all Python-first. No other language comes close.

items.title: Interactive Shell (REPL)
items.text: The Python REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) lets you run code interactively one line at a time. Jupyter Notebooks extend this into a powerful document-based coding environment.

items.title: Rich Standard Library
items.text: Python's 'batteries included' philosophy means the standard library covers everything — file I/O, networking, JSON, XML, databases, cryptography, and more — without any external packages.

sections.title: How Python Works — CPython, pip, and virtualenv Explained

blocks.text: Understanding CPython, pip, and virtualenv is one of the first — and most important — concepts for every Python beginner. These three tools form the foundation of every Python development workflow.
🐍 CPython — The Python Interpreter

CPython is the reference implementation of Python — the official, most widely-used Python interpreter, written in C. When you download Python from python.org, you get CPython. It compiles your .py source code to bytecode and then executes it in the Python Virtual Machine (PVM). CPython includes the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), which limits true multi-threaded parallelism — though Python 3.13+ offers an experimental free-threaded mode that removes this limitation.
📦 pip — Python Package Manager

pip (Pip Installs Packages) is Python's official package manager. It connects to the PyPI (Python Package Index) repository and lets you install, upgrade, and remove third-party libraries with a single command. pip comes bundled with Python 3.4+ automatically.

items.html: pip install numpy — installs the NumPy library for numerical computing
pip install django — installs the Django web framework
pip uninstall requests — removes the Requests library
pip list — shows all installed packages and their versions
pip freeze > requirements.txt — saves all dependencies to a file for sharing

blocks.text: 🔒 virtualenv — Isolated Python Environments

virtualenv (or the built-in venv module) creates isolated Python environments for each project. This means Project A can use Django 4.2 while Project B uses Django 5.0 — without any conflicts. Every professional Python project uses a virtual environment. Python 3.3+ includes venv in the standard library.

Simple rule to remember: CPython runs your code. pip installs your dependencies. venv isolates your project. The current recommended version is Python 3.13 (or 3.12 LTS), available free from python.org.

pros.title: Easiest Language to Learn
pros.text: Python has the lowest learning curve of any major language. Most beginners write working programs within their first day of learning.

pros.title: Dominates AI & Data Science
pros.text: TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy — all Python. If you want to work in AI/ML, Python is non-negotiable.

pros.title: Massive Ecosystem
pros.text: PyPI has 450,000+ packages. Whatever problem you have, there is almost certainly a Python package that solves it.

pros.title: Extremely Versatile
pros.text: Web development, data science, automation, scripting, DevOps, game development, scientific computing — Python does it all.

pros.title: Huge Community
pros.text: Python has one of the largest, most welcoming developer communities. Stack Overflow, Reddit r/learnpython, Discord — help is always available.

pros.title: Rapid Development
pros.text: Python developers typically write 3-5x fewer lines of code than Java or C++ for equivalent functionality, dramatically speeding up development.

pros.title: Excellent for Automation
pros.text: Python is the language of DevOps and automation. Ansible, Fabric, and countless CI/CD tools are Python-based.

pros.title: Free & Open Source
pros.text: Python is 100% free and open-source under the PSF License. Zero cost to start, forever.

cons.title: Slow Execution Speed
cons.text: Python is significantly slower than Java, C++, or Rust for CPU-intensive tasks due to its interpreted nature and the GIL.

cons.title: GIL Limitation
cons.text: The Global Interpreter Lock prevents true multi-threaded CPU parallelism in CPython. Python 3.13+ experimental free-threaded mode is addressing this.

cons.title: High Memory Consumption
cons.text: Python objects carry significant overhead. Python programs typically use 5-10x more memory than equivalent C/C++ programs.

cons.title: Weak for Mobile Development
cons.text: Python has no strong native mobile app framework. Kivy and BeeWare exist but are not mainstream compared to Swift or Kotlin.

cons.title: Runtime Errors
cons.text: Dynamic typing means type errors that Java would catch at compile time only appear in Python when that line actually executes — requiring thorough testing.

cons.title: Not Ideal for Frontend Web
cons.text: Python cannot run in browsers. Web frontend is dominated by JavaScript. Python is back-end only for web development.

sections.title: Where is Python Used? — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: Python's extraordinary versatility makes it the language of choice across more domains than any other programming language. Here are the major areas where Python is actively used in 2026:

items.text: — Python is the universal language of AI. TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras, scikit-learn, and Hugging Face Transformers are all Python-first. Every major AI breakthrough — GPT, Gemini, DALL-E — was built using Python. If you want to work in AI, Python is non-negotiable.

— Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Plotly make Python the tool of choice for data analysts and scientists worldwide. Jupyter Notebooks provide an interactive, document-based environment for data exploration. Netflix, Spotify, and Airbnb use Python for data analysis and recommendation engines.

— Django (batteries-included framework) and Flask/FastAPI (microframeworks) power millions of websites. Instagram, Pinterest, Dropbox, and Reddit were all built on Django. FastAPI is becoming the standard for building high-performance REST APIs and microservices.

— Python is the language of automation. From simple file renaming scripts to complex test automation frameworks (pytest, Selenium), DevOps pipelines (Ansible, Fabric), and web scraping (BeautifulSoup, Scrapy) — Python automates repetitive tasks across every industry.

— AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, and Azure Functions all support Python as a first-class language. Infrastructure-as-code tools like Pulumi and CDK, cloud CLIs, and deployment automation scripts are predominantly Python.

— SciPy, SymPy, and BioPython make Python the primary language in physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering research. NASA, CERN, and major universities use Python for simulations, data analysis, and scientific modelling.

— Python is the dominant language in cybersecurity. Tools like Metasploit, Scapy, and Volatility are Python-based. Security professionals use Python to write exploits, analyse malware, build network scanners, and automate penetration testing.
— Pygame is a popular Python library for 2D game development. Python is the most used language for teaching programming in schools and universities worldwide due to its simplicity and readability.

blocks.text: These are the most commonly asked Python interview questions for freshers and beginner-level positions. Master these before any Python interview.

items.q: Q1. What is Python and what are its key characteristics?
items.a: Python is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. Its key characteristics are: easy-to-read syntax using indentation, dynamic typing (no variable type declarations), interpreted execution (line-by-line), multi-paradigm (OOP + functional + procedural), automatic memory management, and an enormous ecosystem of libraries via PyPI.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between CPython, pip, and venv?
items.a: CPython is the official Python interpreter — it runs your Python code. pip is Python's package manager — it installs third-party libraries from PyPI. venv (or virtualenv) creates isolated Python environments so different projects can have different dependency versions without conflicts. In every Python project: CPython runs it, pip manages libraries, venv isolates it.

items.q: Q3. What is the GIL in Python?
items.a: GIL stands for Global Interpreter Lock. It is a mutex (lock) in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, even on multi-core systems. This means Python threads cannot achieve true CPU parallelism — for CPU-bound tasks, Python uses multiprocessing instead. Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded mode (no GIL) to address this limitation.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
items.a: Lists are mutable (can be changed after creation) and use square brackets: my_list = [1, 2, 3]. Tuples are immutable (cannot be changed) and use parentheses: my_tuple = (1, 2, 3). Use lists when you need to modify the collection. Use tuples for fixed data (like coordinates, RGB values, database records) — they are faster and use less memory than lists.

items.q: Q5. What is PEP 8 in Python?
items.a: PEP 8 is Python's official Style Guide for Python Code. It defines conventions for writing readable Python code — indentation (4 spaces), line length (79 characters max), naming conventions (snake_case for variables/functions, PascalCase for classes), whitespace rules, and comment formatting. Following PEP 8 is expected in professional Python development.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between '==' and 'is' in Python?
items.a: == checks value equality — whether two objects have the same value. 'is' checks identity equality — whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. Example: a = [1,2,3]; b = [1,2,3]. Here a == b is True (same values) but a is b is False (different objects). Common trap: small integers (-5 to 256) and short strings are cached by CPython, so 'is' may return True unexpectedly for them.

items.q: Q7. What is a Python decorator?
items.a: A decorator is a function that takes another function as input, adds functionality to it, and returns the modified function. It is applied using the @ syntax above a function definition. Example: @login_required above a view function checks if a user is logged in before running the view. Python's built-in decorators include @staticmethod, @classmethod, and @property.

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between Python 2 and Python 3?
items.a: Python 2 reached end-of-life in January 2020 and should never be used for new projects. Key differences: In Python 3, print is a function print() not a statement. Integer division (/) returns a float in Python 3 (3/2 = 1.5), not an integer (Python 2: 3/2 = 1). All strings are Unicode in Python 3. range() returns an iterator (not a list) in Python 3. Python 3 has better async support, type hints, and performance.

items.q: Q9. What is the latest version of Python in 2026?
items.a: The latest stable version is Python 3.13 (released October 2024), which introduced an experimental free-threaded mode (no GIL) and a JIT compiler preview. Python 3.12 is the recommended version for production in 2026 due to its stability and excellent performance improvements. Python follows an annual release cycle with new versions each October.

items.q: Q10. What is list comprehension in Python?
items.a: List comprehension is a concise, Pythonic way to create lists in a single line. Syntax: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. Example: squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)] creates [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]. This replaces a for loop + append pattern with one readable line. Python also has dict comprehension, set comprehension, and generator expressions using the same syntax.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Python fundamentals with these practice questions. Try to answer each one before revealing the answer — active recall is the most effective way to learn.

items.q: 1. What does the acronym PVM stand for and what is its role in Python?
items.a: PVM stands for Python Virtual Machine. It is the runtime engine inside CPython that actually executes Python bytecode. When you run a .py file, CPython first compiles it to bytecode (.pyc), then the PVM reads and executes each bytecode instruction one by one. The PVM is what makes Python cross-platform — the same bytecode can run on Windows, Linux, or macOS.

items.q: 2. What is the output of: print(type(3 / 2)) in Python 3?
items.a: <class 'float'>. In Python 3, the / operator always performs float division. 3 / 2 = 1.5 (a float). To get integer division in Python 3, use // (floor division): 3 // 2 = 1 (an int). This was a major change from Python 2 where 3 / 2 = 1 (integer division by default).

items.q: 3. What is the minimum software required to run a Python script on a new computer?
items.a: Just the Python interpreter (CPython) — available free from python.org. Unlike Java, Python has no separate 'runtime' and 'development kit' distinction. The same python installation is used for both running and developing Python programs. For third-party packages, you also need pip (which comes bundled with Python 3.4+).

items.q: 4. What happens when you use a mutable default argument in a Python function?
items.a: It is one of Python's most famous gotchas. Example: def add_item(item, lst=[]). The default [] is created once when the function is defined, not each time it is called. All calls share the same list object. Calling add_item(1) then add_item(2) results in lst being [1, 2] on the second call, not [2]. The Pythonic fix is: def add_item(item, lst=None): if lst is None: lst = []

items.q: 5. Explain the difference between deep copy and shallow copy in Python.
items.a: Shallow copy creates a new object but inserts references to the objects found in the original. Changes to nested objects affect both copies. Deep copy creates a new object and recursively copies all nested objects — completely independent. Use copy.copy() for shallow copy and copy.deepcopy() for deep copy. For a flat list, list slicing (lst[:]) also creates a shallow copy.

items.q: 6. Why is Python slow compared to Java or C++, and how can you speed it up?
items.a: Python is slower because: (1) It is interpreted — bytecode execution is slower than native machine code. (2) Dynamic typing means type checks happen at runtime. (3) The GIL limits multi-threaded CPU parallelism. Solutions: Use NumPy/Pandas (written in C) for number crunching. Use multiprocessing for CPU-bound tasks. Use Cython or Numba to compile Python to C. Use PyPy (JIT-compiled Python, up to 10x faster). For IO-bound tasks, async/await achieves high concurrency without the GIL being a bottleneck.

items.q: 7. What is the output of: print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) in Python?
items.a: False. This is a floating-point precision issue that exists in virtually every programming language that uses IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic (Java, JavaScript, C++ — all have the same issue). 0.1 + 0.2 in Python equals 0.30000000000000004 due to binary representation limitations. The correct way to compare floats is: abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 1e-9, or use Python's decimal.Decimal for exact decimal arithmetic.

items.q: 8. What is the difference between *args and **kwargs in Python?
items.a: *args allows a function to accept any number of positional arguments as a tuple. Example: def func(*args) called as func(1, 2, 3) — args becomes (1, 2, 3). **kwargs allows a function to accept any number of keyword arguments as a dictionary. Example: def func(**kwargs) called as func(name='Alice', age=30) — kwargs becomes {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30}. Both can be combined: def func(*args, **kwargs) accepts any combination of positional and keyword arguments.

sections.title: Conclusion — Is Python Right for You?

blocks.text: Python is not just a programming language — it is the lingua franca of modern computing. From the AI models powering ChatGPT and Gemini to the data pipelines at Netflix and Spotify, from NASA's scientific simulations to the automation scripts running in millions of DevOps pipelines — Python is the common thread.

If you are a complete beginner, Python is universally regarded as the best first language — its minimal syntax lets you focus on learning programming logic, not fighting syntax rules. If you are an experienced developer looking to enter AI/ML, data science, or web backend development, Python is your fastest and most direct path.

items.q: Is Python easy to learn for beginners?
items.a: Yes — Python is consistently ranked the easiest programming language to learn for beginners. Its clean, English-like syntax and minimal boilerplate mean most beginners can write working programs within their first day. Python is the most recommended first programming language by universities, bootcamps, and self-taught developers worldwide.

items.q: What is the difference between Python and Java?
items.a: Python is dynamically typed, interpreted, and prioritises developer speed and code readability. Java is statically typed, compiled to bytecode, and prioritises performance and enterprise reliability. Python is better for AI/ML, data science, and rapid prototyping. Java is better for large-scale enterprise systems, Android development, and high-performance backend services.

items.q: How long does it take to learn Python?
items.a: With consistent daily practice, you can learn Python basics (syntax, data types, functions, OOP) in 3–4 weeks. Becoming proficient including file handling, modules, and standard library takes about 2–3 months. To master advanced Python — decorators, concurrency, testing, and a framework like Django or FastAPI — expect 6–12 months of dedicated learning and project building.

items.q: Is Python free to use in 2026?
items.a: Yes. Python is 100% free and open-source under the PSF (Python Software Foundation) License — one of the most permissive open-source licenses. You can use Python for personal projects, education, and commercial production systems at zero cost. The entire ecosystem (pip, venv, VS Code, PyCharm Community) is also free.

items.q: Should I learn Python 3.12 or 3.13 in 2026?
items.a: For most beginners and production work — start with Python 3.12. It offers excellent stability. Try Python 3.13+ only if you need experimental free-threading features.

items.q: Python vs Java — Which is better in 2026?
items.a: Both are excellent and remain in the top 3 most popular languages globally. Choose Python for AI/ML, data science, automation, scripting, and rapid prototyping. Choose Java for large-scale enterprise backend systems, Android development, and big data engineering (Hadoop, Kafka, Spark). Many professional developers know both — Python for data work, Java for backend services.
